question: The closure of the transitional shelter for psychoactive substance users – the only temporary accommodation structure for homeless drug addicts in Athens – is yet another dangerous development for people with substance misuse problems.

This is another consequence of the implementation of EU guidelines, which the Nea Dimokratia Government is enforcing – as did SYRIZA before it – with the recent law on the ‘completion of the Psychiatric Reform’.

There has already been a push to end treatment programmes and break the continuum of care (advice-treatment-social reintegration) through the establishment of the National Organisation for Preventing and Combating Addiction (EOPAE). Facilities were brutally deprived of experienced staff following a wave of unexpected staff transfers last year.

No provision is made for people with a dual diagnosis of drug dependence and mental illness to be able to join a Therapeutic Community. The fatal blow to Therapeutic Communities came with the 24-hour shifts imposed on the staff, which essentially turned these environments into ‘first aid stations’, bringing about a detrimental change in the working conditions of staff.

Given the need to take substantial measures to prevent drug addiction, for comprehensive, public, free addiction services and to support and expand ‘dry’ addiction programme units, what is the Commission’s position regarding the fact that EU policy – which is based on socalled ‘harm reduction’ and substitution treatments and which every single bourgeois government has implemented over the years on the basis of the ‘cost-benefit’ criterion, including in the field of detoxification – deliberately perpetuates drug dependence, with no meaningful measures being taken to address the issue effectively and help users and their families?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.10.2026) Protecting public health and addressing drug-related harms are key pillars of the EU Drugs Strategy1, adopted by the Commission in December 2025 and endorsed by the Member States in March 20262.
The Strategy lays down measures aimed at reducing drug use, providing accessible treatment for everyone, and supporting the recovery and social reintegration of people with drug use disorders.

The Strategy notably encourages Member States to step up universal and environmental health prevention and develop and implement evidence-based prevention activities specifically designed for groups in vulnerable situations, as well as to strengthen the availability of evidence-based treatment options integrated in a continuum of care.

Across the EU, harm reduction interventions are supported by an extensive body of scientific evidence demonstrating their effectiveness in reducing drug-related harms. These are recognised at both European and international levels, including through successive EU Drugs Strategies and relevant United Nations resolutions. Mental health is also a priority for the Commission.

In 2023, the Commission adopted a Communication on a Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health3, with 20 ambitious flagships linked to almost EUR 1.3 billion in funding opportunities, and with a focus on supporting vulnerable groups.
